summary: A 1969 note making two suggestions for reducing congestion at hosts that swap programs in and out of memory. One is to let the host control the order in which the IMP delivers messages, so it does not waste time swapping a user out and in. It is a proposal, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 19 proposes two ways for slower hosts to spend less time swapping programs in and out of memory. One changes which waiting message a host accepts first; the other keeps a program in memory during a short file transfer.

questions: reduce congestion at swap bound nodes
how did early arpanet hosts handle congestion
subtitle: Two proposed ways to reduce swapping delays at slow ARPANET hosts.

tldr.problem: Hosts with slower transfers between core memory and auxiliary storage could waste time processing messages in an inconvenient order.
tldr.mechanism: The note proposes letting a host choose the order of queued messages, or having cooperating hosts lock programs in core during a multi-message file transfer.
tldr.outcome: The note presents both ideas for consideration; it does not say they were adopted.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 19 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text presents two suggestions for consideration and does not state whether they were adopted.

sections.title: Why Message Order Could Waste Time
sections.content:
Hosts differed in how quickly they could move programs between core memory and auxiliary storage. When an IMP delivered messages in the order it received them, a host might have to swap one user's program out and another in, then reverse that work for the next message.

The note suggests that reducing this swapping could improve network use for slower hosts and other nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can waste time moving programs in and out of memory when messages arrive for users in an inconvenient order. The note explores ways to reduce that extra work.

sections.title: Let the Host Choose the Next Message
sections.content:
The first proposal would let a host read the IMP's queue of waiting messages and accept them in the order it finds most effective. For example, the host could accept a message for a user whose program is already in core instead of first swapping in another user's program.

The author notes that this change would affect BBN's IMP software.
sections.plainLanguage: The host could choose a waiting message for a program already in memory. This could avoid swapping programs just to follow the IMP's arrival order.

sections.title: Keep Programs in Memory During a Transfer
sections.content:
The second proposal is for cooperating hosts to lock the needed programs in core during a multi-message file transfer over an auxiliary connection. The author estimates that a 50-kilobit-per-second line used at 100% efficiency would carry just over 6 messages of 8 kilobits each per second.

The note says keeping a program in core for more than about 2 seconds may be unsuitable in a time-sharing environment. On that assumption, this approach would fit only files of 2-16 messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Two hosts could keep the needed programs in memory while sending a file. The note says this would suit only a limited file size because a program should not stay locked in memory too long.

sections.title: Suggestions for Consideration
sections.content:
RFC 19 offers two protocol suggestions: host-controlled selection from the IMP's queue, and core-to-core transfers with programs locked during the transfer. The author points out that the second proposal has a narrow useful range under the stated assumptions.

The note recommends considering the ideas but does not record an adoption decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The document offers two possible ways to reduce swapping overhead. It explains a limit on the second idea but does not say whether either proposal was adopted.
